reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: A biochemically defined group unified by raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid (and often 3-methylglutaric acid), but with several genetically and clinically distinct entities

Type I reflects a true defect of leucine catabolism (3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase, AUH gene); the other types are secondary and largely relate to disturbed mitochondrial membrane/phospholipid biology rather than the leucine pathway
Type II is Barth syndrome (X-linked, TAZ gene) with cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia, and growth delay
Type III is Costeff optic atrophy syndrome (OPA3) with early optic atrophy and later movement disorder, described notably in individuals of Iraqi-Jewish descent
So-called type IV is a heterogeneous group of mitochondrial disorders sharing the biochemical marker, and DNAJC19-related dilated cardiomyopathy with ataxia is another form
The 3-methylglutaconate elevation in the secondary forms is usually modest and is a clue to a mitochondrial membrane problem rather than the primary defect itself
Management is form-specific and supportive, including cardiac care in Barth syndrome and ophthalmological care in Costeff syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA is an intermediate of leucine degradation, normally hydrated by 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase before onward metabolism. In type I 3-methylglutaconic aciduria this enzyme is deficient, so 3-methylglutaconate and 3-methylglutarate accumulate. In the other, more common types the enzyme is intact and the raised 3-methylglutaconate arises secondarily from disturbed mitochondrial inner-membrane function and phospholipid (cardiolipin) metabolism, as in Barth syndrome where tafazzin deficiency impairs cardiolipin remodelling. Thus the shared biochemical marker points either to a discrete leucine-pathway block or, more often, to a broader mitochondrial membrane disorder with the specific clinical consequences of the underlying gene.
additionalDifferentials: Other organic acidurias of leucine metabolism (e.g. 3-methylglutaconyl versus 3-methylcrotonyl defects)
Other causes of infantile or childhood cardiomyopathy
Secondary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria from acquired mitochondrial stress
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids quantifying 3-methylglutaconic and 3-methylglutaric acids
Echocardiography and cardiac assessment (especially for Barth syndrome)
Targeted molecular testing (AUH, TAZ, OPA3, DNAJC19 and mitochondrial genes)
Cardiolipin/monolysocardiolipin analysis where Barth syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Cardiomyopathy or heart failure, particularly in a male infant (Barth syndrome)
Severe or cyclical neutropenia with infection risk
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy
Neurological regression suggesting a mitochondrial disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the specific type: Barth syndrome outcome hinges on cardiac and infective complications, Costeff syndrome causes progressive visual and motor impairment, and type I ranges from mild to more significant neurological involvement. Care is directed at the underlying entity.
pitfalls: Treating the biochemical finding as a single disease rather than pursuing the specific underlying genetic cause
Missing Barth syndrome in a boy with cardiomyopathy and neutropenia
Assuming a primary leucine-pathway defect when most cases are secondary mitochondrial disorders
Overlooking optic atrophy in the Costeff phenotype
references: Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Management directed at the specific underlying entity identified rather than the shared biochemical marker, as there is no single disease-specific therapy.
For Barth syndrome, standard heart-failure treatment for the cardiomyopathy, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for neutropenia, and vigilant treatment of infection.
For Costeff (type III) syndrome, low-vision support for the optic atrophy and symptomatic management of the movement disorder.
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography, full blood count monitoring for neutropenia, and ophthalmological review for optic atrophy.
Multidisciplinary input from cardiology, haematology, ophthalmology and metabolic medicine according to the subtype.
Genetic counselling tailored to the mode of inheritance, X-linked for Barth syndrome and autosomal recessive for the other forms, with family screening.
Early escalation for cardiac decompensation or for sepsis in neutropenic Barth syndrome.
